newsitem.title: INDIA: FOCUS-Indian stocks turn from politics to Reliance.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Indian stocks turn from politics to Reliance.

text.p: Indian stocks paused for breath on Tuesday as political fears evaporated and the spotlight turned to a key earnings announcement from top private firm Reliance Industries, analysts said.
They said the country's volatile stock markets would trade narrowly as new Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral looked set to win a trust vote due later in the day.
"I think the market will take a breather," said Partha Roy Chowdhury, assistant director, equity trading, at securities firm Peregrine Capital in Hong Kong.
"There were enough investors who were betting that a new government would be formed and that the budget would get passed. They bought when the index was at 3300-3400 levels," he said.
Bombay's benchmark stocks index closed 0.84 points, or 0.02 percent, higher at 3800.63.
Shares in Delhi and Calcutta closed mixed after rangebound trade. The National Stock Exchange index ended a touch lower.
Bombay's index had jumped nearly 40 points, or one percent, to 3839.54 in morning trade ahead of the Reliance results.
The spotlight was on the petrochemicals giant which said its net rose to 13.23 billion rupees in the financial year ended March 31, 1997, from 13.05 billion a year earlier.
The results were sharply above the consensus estimate of 12.06 billion rupees, according to a Reuter poll.
Reliance shares -- which surged almost 10 percent on Monday in the run-up to the results -- ended 0.25 rupees higher at 308 as speculators booked profits after the announcement.
The company's shares ended near their previous close on the Delhi and National exchanges.
Analysts said the focus would now shift to key earnings for the 1996/97 financial year due in the coming months.
"At this point we're asking investors to wait. The market should ease, it has run up a little too much," said Sandeep Nanda, head of research at Natwest Markets.
"Poor results will start coming in next month."

Bombay's widely-tracked stocks index has surged 13 percent since March 31, when the Congress party triggered the crisis by withdrawing key support to the 10-month-old ruling alliance and lopped eight percent off the index that day.

"Another 100 points up and this market will be a sell," said the head of sales at a foreign brokerage. "Lots of investors have been sitting on paper and they are bound to book profits at higher levels."

Congress has promised to back Gujral through the remaining four years of the government's term. Politicians say the 1997/98 (April-March) pro-business federal budget -- held hostage to the crisis -- is also likely to be approved by parliament.
"There don't appear to be any further surprises on the political front. The budget is likely to be passed and we see some profit-booking taking place," Peregrine's Chowdhury said.
Analysts said disappointing results from leading firms in sectors like cement and steel due to a slowdown in demand and weak global prices of commodities would make investors gloomy.

"We are entering a reporting season in which earnings growth may well turn out to be in single digits, suggesting that the slowdown was even sharper than originally estimated," U.S. investment bank Lehman Brothers said in its latest weekly note.
Lehman cautioned that the near-term resolution of the government crisis did not remove the possibility of more political tremors later in the year.

"Having entered 1997 with increasing confidence that the government may enjoy a longer lease of life than initially anticipated, recent events have considerably eroded confidence regarding political stability," Lehman said, keeping its "neutral" weighting on the country. --Bombay newsroom, (91) 22 265 9000
